content:
Happy Eid Mubarak, 
hashtag
#Eid Milad-un-Nabi Mubarak...

I’ve been seeing these greetings across social media platforms and in my inbox.

In the bleak and often divisive times we live in, such messages are genuinely heartening. So, thank you so much for them ❤️

Since many people have asked about it or are wondering “yeh kaun si wali Eid hai?” because most Muslims are working today and it is not observed on the scale of Eid-ul-Fitr or Eid-ul-Azha (commonly known as Eid and Bakrid), here’s a brief note: 

Unlike Eid-ul-Fitr and Eid-ul-Azha, which are the two most important Islamic festivals, Milad-un-Nabi is observed differently across Muslim communities and regions. It is not marked by the same level of celebration everywhere.

For instance, while growing up in Bihar’s Kosi region, we referred to this day as Bara-Wafat. Some people also called it Barah Rabi-ul-Awwal. There were, and largely still are, no major public celebrations associated with it.

In many other parts of the country, however, it has been celebrated with great enthusiasm for centuries as Jashn-e-Milad-un-Nabi. 

A case in point is Pune, where last year the city witnessed the 1500th edition of Jashn-e-Eid Milad-un-Nabi organised by the local Seerat Committee. In fact, several Seerat Committees across India have histories stretching back generations.

In short, the celebration of Eid Milad-un-Nabi is not new, and juloos (processions) have long been an integral part of its observance in many places.

But why is it celebrated?

It commemorates the birth of Prophet Muhammad (PBUH), the last Prophet of Islam. Moreover, according to some riwayaat (traditional accounts), Prophet Muhammad is also believed to have passed away on the same date, 12 Rabi-ul-Awwal.

Enough of the gyaan, right? Let me leave you with a few couplets from two beautiful naats (poems written in praise of Prophet Muhammad):

Jashn-e-Amad-e-Rasool Allah Hi Allah
Bibi Amina Ke Phool Allah Hi Allah

Jab Ke Sarkaar Tashreef Laane Lage
Hoor-o-Gilman Bhi Khushiyan Manaane Lage

Har Taraf Noor Ki Roshni Chha Gayi
Mustafa Kya Mile, Zindagi Mil Gayi

Ae Halima Teri God Mein Aa Gayi
Dono Aalam Ke Rasool Allah Hi Allah

---

Hum kisi deen se hon, qaayal-e-kirdaar to hain
Hum sana-khwaan-e-Shah-e-Haider-e-Karrar to hain

Naamleva hain Muhammad ke parastaar to hain
Yaani majboor paye Ahmad-e-Mukhtar to hain

Ishq ho jaaye kisi se, koi chaara to nahin
Sirf Muslim ka Muhammad pe ijara to nahin

The author of the first naat is unclear to me. The second one is by Kunwar Mohinder Singh Bedi “Sahar”, one of the finest Urdu poets of the subcontinent.

Eid Milad-un-Nabi Mubarak!
comment: The way communities observe traditions often reflects local history and lived realities. Recognizing these variations can help institutions build more inclusive cultural understanding beyond labels and assumptions.
